239.title: Kena Upanishad (one week): who impels the mind? (1 of 7)
239.word: the story of the gods and Brahman
239.hook: a whole Upanishad that begins with a question a child might ask
239.tomorrow: Kena Upanishad (one week): who impels the mind? (2 of 7)
239.howItsDone: The Kena Upanishad is studied in Hindu Vedanta traditions as a short, central text; its opening question, 'kena?', by whom?, is often used as a starting point for self-inquiry.

screen: `DAY TWO-HUNDRED-THIRTY-NINE.`

segments.voice: Last week, the whole Isha in eighteen verses: renounce and enjoy. All this pervaded by the Lord, and the face of truth covered with gold. Did you look past one golden lid? Day two hundred thirty-nine.
screen: `RENOUNCE AND ENJOY.`

segments.voice: Small children ask the best questions, right up until we teach them to stop. Why is the sky blue? Where was I before I was born? And sometimes, lying in bed: who's thinking my thoughts? Most of us laughed that one off by age ten. This week's Upanishad doesn't. It opens with exactly that question, asked by a student to a teacher, and it takes it completely seriously. It's called the Kena, and like the Isha it's named after its first word. Kena means: by whom?
screen: `WHO'S THINKING MY THOUGHTS?` → `THE QUESTION WE STOP ASKING.` → `KENA: BY WHOM?`

segments.voice: Here is the first verse, the student's question. By whom willed, by whom sent, does the mind fly out to its objects? By whom commanded does the first breath move? By whom impelled do people speak this speech? And what god sets the eye and the ear to their work? Four questions. Mind, breath, speech, eye and ear. Notice what they have in common. They're the things you think of as you. Your thinking, your breathing, your talking, your seeing. And the question asks: who's behind them? What makes the mind go? Think about it for a second. You didn't decide to have your next thought. It just arrived. You don't usually decide to breathe; it breathes. Your ear hears the traffic whether you want it to or not. So who, or what, is doing the doing? The Kena comes from the Sama Veda, the Veda of chanted song, and it's short: four sections, a few dozen verses. The first two sections are the teacher's answer, in paradoxes. The last two sections tell a story: the gods win a battle, take the credit, and meet a mysterious being they can't recognize. That story is our word for the week, the story of the gods and Brahman, and we'll get to it on day five. But first the question has to land. Brahman, which you've met before, is the tradition's word for the ultimate reality, the ground of everything. The Kena is going to say that Brahman is the answer to by whom. Not a thing the mind can grab. The one the mind runs on.

segments.voice: Two minutes. Sit, close your eyes, and just watch for the next thought. Don't make one. Wait for it. When it comes, notice: you didn't order it. It arrived. Then watch for the next one. Between them, if there's a gap, rest there. You can gently ask the Kena's question, not to answer it, just to hold it: by whom? Then go back to watching. The bell holds the time.
The story of the gods and Brahman. This week's word, from the Kena Upanishad. The story comes later in the week; today, its question: by whom does the mind fly out?
screen: `THE STORY OF THE GODS AND BRAHMAN — today's word`.

240.title: Kena Upanishad (one week): who impels the mind? (2 of 7)
240.word: the story of the gods and Brahman
240.hook: the ear of the ear, the mind of the mind
240.tomorrow: Kena Upanishad (one week): who impels the mind? (3 of 7)
240.howItsDone: In Vedanta teaching, Kena 1.2 ('the ear of the ear, the mind of the mind') is often used to point students toward awareness itself as distinct from what it perceives.

screen: `DAY TWO-HUNDRED-FORTY.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Kena's question: by whom does the mind fly out? Your line was the one behind the ear. Did you ask, once, what was doing the hearing? Day two hundred forty.
screen: `KENA: BY WHOM?`

segments.voice: Think about a movie theater. You watch the whole film, the car chase, the kiss, the explosion, and you never once look at the light. But without the projector's beam, there's nothing on the screen at all. Every image you see is made of it, and it's the one thing you don't see. Yesterday the student asked who makes the mind go. Today the teacher answers. And the answer sounds, at first, like a riddle. It's really a description of the light in the projector.
screen: `THE MOVIE AND THE LIGHT.` → `THE ONE THING YOU DON'T SEE.` → `THE TEACHER ANSWERS.`

segments.voice: Verse two. It is the ear of the ear. The mind of the mind. The speech of speech. The breath of breath. The eye of the eye. Shrotrasya shrotram: the hearing of hearing. What does that mean? Your ear hears sounds. But something is aware of the hearing itself: something knows that you are hearing. That's the ear of the ear. Your mind thinks thoughts. Something is aware of the thinking. That's the mind of the mind. The Kena is pointing past each sense to the awareness it runs on, the way you'd point past the picture to the light. That's the carry for the week: the one behind the ear. Then the verse adds that the wise, letting go of the idea that the senses are all there is, go beyond this world and become deathless. Here's why this matters on an ordinary day. We usually identify with what's on the screen. I'm angry. I'm tired. I'm this worry. The Kena says: the anger is a picture. You're closer to the light it's shown in. That doesn't make the anger fake, and it doesn't mean you shouldn't deal with it. It means there's a place in you the anger doesn't reach. The ear of the ear isn't hurt by a harsh word. It just hears it. Different schools explain this light differently, but the Vedanta traditions agree it's here: not far away, not somewhere you travel to, but behind every single thing you notice today.

segments.voice: Two minutes. Close your eyes and listen to the sounds around you: a fan, traffic, your own breath. Let them come. Now, instead of the sounds, notice the hearing. Something is aware that sound is happening. Rest there for a few breaths, in the listening rather than in the sounds. If a thought pulls you away, notice that something is aware of the thought too. Then come back to the listening. The bell holds the time.
The story of the gods and Brahman. Before the story, the answer: Brahman is the ear of the ear, the mind of the mind, the breath of breath.

241.title: Kena Upanishad (one week): who impels the mind? (3 of 7)
241.word: the story of the gods and Brahman
241.hook: the eye cannot go there, nor speech, nor the mind
241.tomorrow: Kena Upanishad (one week): who impels the mind? (4 of 7)
241.howItsDone: Hindus who study Vedanta often learn the Kena's refrain (1.4–1.8) as a teaching that Brahman is the knower, never an object known, alongside continuing worship of God in images and names.

screen: `DAY TWO-HUNDRED-FORTY-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: the ear of the ear, the mind of the mind. Your line, the one behind the ear. Did you take one breath behind the listening? Day two hundred forty-one.
screen: `THE EAR OF THE EAR.`

segments.voice: Try to see your own eyes. Not in a mirror, that's a picture. Your actual eyes, the ones doing the seeing. You can't. They're the one thing in your field of vision that can never be in your field of vision. Try to taste your own tongue. Same problem. The Kena's next verses start from this puzzle. If Brahman is the eye of the eye, then the eye will never see it. And then the text says something that sounds almost shocking for a sacred book.
screen: `TRY TO SEE YOUR OWN EYES.` → `THE ONE THING NEVER IN VIEW.` → `A SHOCKING LINE.`

segments.voice: Verse three: the eye does not go there, nor speech, nor the mind. We don't know it, we don't understand how anyone could teach it. It is other than the known, and beyond the unknown. So we have heard from the ancients who explained it to us. Notice the honesty. The teacher says: we can't hand this to you like an object. Then verses four to eight, five times over, a refrain. That which speech cannot express, but by which speech is expressed: know that alone as Brahman, not this that people worship here. That which the mind cannot think, but by which the mind thinks. That which the eye cannot see, but by which the eyes see. The ear, the breath, the same. Know that alone as Brahman, not this that people worship here. What does that line mean? Commentators don't read it as throwing out worship. Hindus go right on worshiping, and the Kena itself will soon tell a story about the gods. The point is sharper: whatever you can set in front of you as an object, even a holy one, is not the one doing the seeing. Shankara reads it that way: Brahman is never an object among objects; it's the subject of all of them. So the image on the altar, the word in the prayer, can point to it. They can't contain it. Like a finger pointing at the moon, which is useful exactly as long as you don't mistake it for the moon.
screen: `THE EYE DOES NOT GO THERE.` · `OTHER THAN THE KNOWN, BEYOND THE UNKNOWN.` · `BY WHICH THE EYES SEE.` · `NOT AN OBJECT, THE SEER OF OBJECTS.` · then, large: `KNOW THAT ALONE AS BRAHMAN.`

segments.voice: Two minutes. Open your eyes softly and look at something in front of you. Notice all you can see. Now, without moving your eyes, notice that the seeing is happening from somewhere you can't see. You'll never catch it in view. Close your eyes and do the same with a thought: watch it, and notice you can't turn around and watch the watcher. Don't strain. Just rest in not being able to catch it. The bell holds the time.
The story of the gods and Brahman. Before we reach the story, the Kena's refrain: that by which the eyes see, know that alone as Brahman.
screen: `THE STORY OF THE GODS AND BRAHMAN — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the one behind the ear. Today, when you look at something beautiful, remember the one looking is never in the picture. Day two hundred forty-one.

242.title: Kena Upanishad (one week): who impels the mind? (4 of 7)
242.word: the story of the gods and Brahman
242.hook: whoever thinks they know it doesn't
242.tomorrow: Kena Upanishad (one week): who impels the mind? (5 of 7)
242.howItsDone: Hindu teachers often quote Kena 2.3, 'it is unknown to those who know', to warn students against treating Brahman as something the intellect can possess.

screen: `DAY TWO-HUNDRED-FORTY-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: the eye does not go there. That by which the eyes see, know that alone as Brahman. Your line, the one behind the ear. Day two hundred forty-two.
screen: `THE EYE DOES NOT GO THERE.`

segments.voice: You've probably met someone who's taken one philosophy class and now has the universe figured out. And you've probably met the opposite: a grandmother, maybe, who has prayed every morning for sixty years, and when you ask what God is, she laughs and says, who knows? Which one knows more? The second section of the Kena is about exactly this. The student hears yesterday's teaching and says, in effect, got it. And the teacher's reply is one of the most famous paradoxes in the Upanishads.
screen: `ONE CLASS, EVERYTHING FIGURED OUT.` → `SIXTY YEARS, WHO KNOWS?` → `GOT IT.`

segments.voice: The teacher says: if you think, I know it well, then surely you know very little of Brahman, only its form in you and in the gods. You'll have to think about it again. The student goes away and thinks. And comes back with this. I don't think, I know it well. And I don't think, I don't know it. Whoever among us understands that, understands it. Then the famous verse: it is known to the one who doesn't claim to know it. The one who claims to know it doesn't know. It is unknown to those who know, and known to those who don't. That can sound like a trick. It isn't. Remember yesterday: Brahman is the knower, never an object. So the moment you say, I've got it, you've turned it into an object, something in your pocket. And whatever's in your pocket isn't it. The knowing the Kena means is more like the knowing you have of being awake. You don't know it the way you know a phone number. You just are awake. Verse four gives a hint: it is known in every act of knowing, pratibodha viditam. Not a special experience, but present in each moment of awareness. And verse five raises the stakes: if you realize it here, in this life, that is the truth; if not, a great loss. The grandmother laughing, who knows? might be closer than the philosophy student. Not because she knows less. Because she isn't trying to put it in her pocket.

segments.voice: Two minutes. Sit, and try something odd: stop trying to understand. For these two minutes, you don't have to get anything. Just be aware. Notice that awareness is already here without you doing anything. You didn't have to earn it. When the mind says, is this it? am I doing it right? let that question go by. The Kena would smile at it. Come back to simply being aware. The bell holds the time.
The story of the gods and Brahman. Tomorrow the story begins. Today, the paradox that sets it up: Brahman is unknown to those who claim to know it.

segments.voice: Your line: the one behind the ear. Today, when you feel sure you've got someone or something completely figured out, leave a little room. Day two hundred forty-two.

243.title: Kena Upanishad (one week): who impels the mind? (5 of 7)
243.word: the story of the gods and Brahman
243.hook: the gods win a victory and take the credit; then a stranger appears
243.tomorrow: Kena Upanishad (one week): who impels the mind? (6 of 7)
243.howItsDone: The Kena's story of Agni and the blade of grass is often retold in Hindu teaching and children's storybooks as a lesson that every power comes from Brahman, and about the danger of pride.

screen: `DAY TWO-HUNDRED-FORTY-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: it is unknown to those who claim to know it. Your line, the one behind the ear. Did you leave a little room around something you were sure of? Day two hundred forty-three.
screen: `UNKNOWN TO THOSE WHO CLAIM IT.`

segments.voice: Picture a team that just won the championship. The locker room is loud. Everyone's giving interviews. I made that shot. My defense won it. Nobody mentions the coach who built the plan, or the groundskeeper, or the thousand things that had to go right. After two sections of paradox, the Kena changes gear completely. It tells a story. And it starts in a locker room, more or less: the gods have just won a great victory, and they're very pleased with themselves.
screen: `THE CHAMPIONSHIP LOCKER ROOM.` → `I MADE THAT SHOT.` → `THE GODS, PLEASED WITH THEMSELVES.`

segments.voice: Section three. Brahman won a victory for the gods. The text doesn't say against whom; tradition says the asuras, the gods' old rivals. But the gods felt great in that victory, and they said: this victory is ours, this greatness is ours. You can hear it. Ours. Brahman knew what they were thinking, and appeared before them. Not as a voice from heaven. As a yaksha: a wondrous, mysterious being, a presence they couldn't place. And they didn't know what it was. So they turned to Agni, the god of fire, the one who knows all beings. Agni, find out what this wondrous being is. Agni ran up to it. The being asked: who are you? I am Agni. I am the one who knows all beings. And what power is in you? I could burn up everything there is, whatever is on this earth. The being set down a single blade of grass. Burn this. Agni rushed at it with all his speed, and couldn't burn it. He came back to the gods: I couldn't find out what this being is. Stop there, because this is the heart of the story, and of the week's word. Fire, who can burn the world, can't burn a blade of grass. Why? Go back to the teaching. Brahman is the fire of fire, the one by which fire burns. Agni's power was never his own. It was on loan. When the one it came from simply held it back, there was nothing left. The story is the Kena's earlier teaching, acted out: the eye of the eye, now as a blade of grass.

segments.voice: Two minutes. Think of something you're proud of: a skill, a win, a talent. Let yourself feel good about it. Now, gently, list what it rested on. Your body working. The people who taught you. The breath you didn't earn. The chance to be born at all. Let the pride stay, but let it widen into thanks. Breathe in: this is mine. Breathe out: this was given. The bell holds the time.
The story of the gods and Brahman. Today it began: the gods take the credit, a wondrous being appears, and fire can't burn a blade of grass.
screen: `THE STORY OF THE GODS AND BRAHMAN — today's word`.

244.title: Kena Upanishad (one week): who impels the mind? (6 of 7)
244.word: the story of the gods and Brahman
244.hook: the wind can't move a blade of grass, and when Indra comes near, the stranger vanishes
244.tomorrow: Kena Upanishad (one week): who impels the mind? (7 of 7)
244.howItsDone: Many Hindus, especially in Shaiva and Shakta traditions, honor Uma Haimavati in the Kena as an early appearance of the goddess, the divine mother who teaches the gods.

screen: `DAY TWO-HUNDRED-FORTY-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the story of the gods and Brahman began. The gods took the credit, a wondrous being appeared, and Agni, who could burn the earth, couldn't burn one blade of grass. Day two hundred forty-four.
screen: `FIRE CANNOT BURN IT.`

segments.voice: You know that moment when you're sure someone else will handle it. The first person failed, fine, but the next one is stronger. Surely they'll crack it. The gods are in exactly that spot. Fire came back empty-handed. So they send the next one, someone with even more reach. And when he fails too, they send their king. What happens to the king is the strangest turn in the whole story. Because he doesn't fail the way the others did.
screen: `THE NEXT ONE WILL CRACK IT.` → `THEN THE WIND.` → `THEN THE KING.`

segments.voice: The gods turn to Vayu, the wind. Vayu, find out what this wondrous being is. He runs up. Who are you? I am Vayu, the one who moves through the sky. What power is in you? I could carry off everything there is, whatever is on this earth. The same blade of grass is set down. Carry this off. Vayu rushes at it with all his speed, and can't move it. He comes back: I couldn't find out. Then the gods turn to Indra, king of the gods. Maghavan, find out what this being is. Indra runs toward it. And the being vanishes. No question, no blade of grass, no test. Just gone. Why vanish for Indra? The text doesn't say, and commentators offer reasons. One common reading: Indra was the proudest of all, the king, so he's made to wait, and learn humility. Another: Indra was already closer, and the next teaching needs a different teacher. Either way, the king is left standing in empty space. And there, in that same space, he meets a woman. The text calls her very radiant, or richly adorned, and names her: Uma, daughter of Himavat, the Himalaya. It's one of the earliest times in Hindu scripture that Uma appears by name, and many later Hindus hear in her the goddess Parvati, Shiva's consort, the divine mother. Indra asks her the question none of the gods could answer: what was that wondrous being? Tomorrow, her answer. For now, notice the turn. Fire and wind tried to measure the mystery by their own power. Indra came nearer, lost the mystery, and was given a teacher.

segments.voice: Two minutes. Think of a time something you were chasing slipped away: an answer, a plan, a feeling of certainty. Stay with the empty space it left. Don't rush to fill it. In the story, the empty space is exactly where the teacher appears. Breathe, and let the space be open. If a thought rushes in to fix things, let it pass, and come back to the open space. The bell holds the time.
The story of the gods and Brahman. The wind can't move the grass; the king comes near and the being vanishes; and Uma appears.
screen: `THE STORY OF THE GODS AND BRAHMAN — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the one behind the ear. Today, when something slips away from you, wait one breath before filling the space. Something might appear there. Day two hundred forty-four.

245.howItsDone: The Kena is often taught as a whole in a week or less in Hindu study circles; Uma's answer, 'it is Brahman', is remembered as the moment the gods learn their power was never their own.

screen: `DAY TWO-HUNDRED-FORTY-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the story of the gods and Brahman went on: the wind couldn't move the grass, the being vanished before Indra, and Uma appeared. Today, her answer. Day two hundred forty-five.
screen: `UMA, DAUGHTER OF THE HIMALAYA.`

segments.voice: Sometimes the truth about a thing only arrives afterward. You find out years later that a teacher quietly paid your school fees. That your parents skipped meals so you could eat. And every memory of that time rearranges itself: oh. It was you, all along. Indra is standing in empty space, beside a radiant woman, and he asks her what that wondrous being was. Her answer rearranges the whole story.
screen: `IT WAS YOU, ALL ALONG.` → `INDRA ASKS.` → `UMA ANSWERS.`

segments.voice: Section four. Uma says: it is Brahman. It was in Brahman's victory that you were glorying. And then Indra knew. That's the whole reveal. The victory the gods called ours was Brahman's. The fire that could burn and the wind that could carry were Brahman's power, lent. The text adds that Agni, Vayu and Indra stand above the other gods because they came nearest to it, and Indra above them all, because he was the first to know it was Brahman. Then the teaching turns inward. How is Brahman glimpsed? Like a flash of lightning. Like the blink of an eye: ah! Brahman isn't held; it flashes, and you're changed. And in yourself? The mind moves toward it, and remembers it, again and again. Then a name to hold onto: tadvanam, which Shankara reads as the one who is adored, the dear one. Meditate on it as the beloved, the text says, and all beings will love such a person. Finally the student asks: teach me the Upanishad. The teacher says: it's been taught. Its foundation is discipline, self-control and work. The Vedas are its limbs. Truth is its home. So here's the week. By whom does the mind fly out? The ear of the ear. The eye doesn't go there. Unknown to those who claim to know. The gods take credit, fire can't burn a blade of grass, wind can't lift it, the king comes near and is given a teacher. And Uma: it was Brahman. The one behind the ear, the one behind the victory, all along.
screen: `IT WAS BRAHMAN'S VICTORY.` · `LIKE A FLASH OF LIGHTNING.` · `TADVANAM: THE DEAR ONE.` · `TRUTH IS ITS HOME.` · then, large: `THE ONE BEHIND THE EAR.`

segments.voice: Two minutes. Think back over this week. Pick one moment when you felt something flash: a sound you really heard, a flinch that softened, a question that opened. Hold it the way the Kena says the mind holds Brahman: coming back to it, again and again. Each time your attention wanders, return to that moment, gently, like returning to someone dear. The bell holds the time.
The story of the gods and Brahman. The gods took the credit; fire and wind failed; Uma told Indra: it was Brahman, and the victory was Brahman's.
screen: `THE STORY OF THE GODS AND BRAHMAN — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the one behind the ear. That's the Kena. Tomorrow, a boy walks into the house of Death. Today, thank someone whose help you didn't see at the time. Day two hundred forty-five.
